units.translation: The same I restored at Sept. 966 = 978 and Ag. 114 (where ἐὲ παπαῖ [alas, alas]) and perhaps should be restored at Suppl. 831, as far as can be judged in a defective passage, for ἠὲ ἡ [or or], which is in the codex, into which the same was also introduced at Pers. 569 = 577 651 = 656, where it is utterly absurd, as I showed in Leutsch's Philologus vol. 13 p. 477 485; and in general this interjection, mentioned by no grammarian, never existed: but the doubled ἢ ἢ [or or] did exist, although only one example survives, Arist. Nub. 105 (which the grammarian uses in Montef. Bibl. Coisl. p. 500 600.) ἢ ἢ σιώπα [or or be silent], which I wrote as one word ἠή [or]. To Sophocles OC. 149 I restored ἐὴ (ἒ ἔ L) [alas], ἀλαῶν ὀμμάτων [of blind eyes], in accordance with the strophic verse 117 ὅρα, τίς ἄρ᾽ ἣν; ποῦ ναίει; [see, who was it? where does he live?]. Tr. 1005 1014, where the codex has ἐ έ [alas], either ἐὴ ἐή [alas alas] or αἰαῖ [alas] should be written. Ib. 1025 ἐὲ ἰὼ ἰὼ δαίμον [alas, oh, oh, god], since a dochmius is read in the antistrophe 1043 τὸν μέλεον φθίσας [having destroyed the wretched one], either ἐὴ ἰὼ δαίμων [alas, oh god] should be written, or, which is more probable, αἰαὶ, ἰὼ δαίμων [alas, oh god], with the second syllable of the interjection shortened, as in the same meter Ant. 1288 αἰαῖ, ὀλωλότ᾽ ἄνδρα [alas, having destroyed the man]. Finally Tr. 1081, where the codex absurdly piles up interjections αἶ αἶ ὦ τάλας αἰ αἰ [alas, alas, oh wretched one, alas, alas] (with the letters ε ε [e e] written over αἰ αἰ [alas alas] by a later hand), I restored the iambic dipody αἰαî τάλας [alas, wretched one]. é é was wrongly introduced at the beginning of the verse Ch. 789. Ib. 869 I wrote ἐὴ ὁτοτοτοῖ [alas, otototoi], where M has ề ễ, but more probable is ἐὴ ἐὴ, ὀτοτοτοτοῖ [alas, alas, ototototoi].
But who of the ill-fated, who, alas, | such as I, toil?
Alas, alas, wretched ones, they gasp on the land.
It cries, it cries within me for my limbs, | the heart within,
alas, new (this monosyllable) and old. = alas, he fares ill,
or give me as food to the sea creatures
see, who was it? where does he live?
alas, alas, oh wretched one, alas, alas

Much more frequent are examples of the other form θέλω [I wish], which will be discussed in its place. The trisyllabic form is used especially in anapaests, the disyllabic in iambic verses, for which the trisyllabic is less 101 convenient. But the imperfect and aorist are consistently taken from the trisyllabic form, as the augment shows, ἤθελον [I was wishing] and ἠθέλησα [I wished].
before he is willing to pay the penalty.
what I must suffer I am willing.
and I obtained by lot the very thing I wished.
But I am willing to accept these things.
for the sake of good deeds I would have wished to become known.

of himself, of herself, of itself
